1	# InventoryRepositoryTest.kt
2	
3	> Source: [src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt](../../../../../src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryRepositoryTest.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-24
4	
5	## Role
6	
7	Tests the repository and the schema against a real Postgres. It checks that SQL results map to
8	`InventoryItem`, that rows come back in order, and that the database's `CHECK` constraint really
9	blocks negative stock. That last test is the "Database backstop" item from the oversell test
10	plan in `.claude/TODO.md`.
11	
12	## Walkthrough
13	
14	### A JDBC test slice
15	
16	```kotlin
17	@JdbcTest
18	@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration::class, InventoryRepository::class)
19	class InventoryRepositoryTest @Autowired constructor(
20	    private val inventoryRepository: InventoryRepository,
21	    private val jdbcClient: JdbcClient,
22	) {
23	```
24	
25	**Spring: `@JdbcTest`, a test *slice*.** `@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application.
26	`@JdbcTest` starts only the database part: the `DataSource`, `JdbcTemplate`/`JdbcClient`,
27	transactions, and Flyway, which creates the table. There are no web beans, and **component
28	scanning is off**, so our own `@Repository` isn't created automatically. That's why
29	`InventoryRepository::class` is listed in `@Import`. The smaller context starts faster, and a
30	failure points straight at the data layer.
31	
32	**Spring: every test is rolled back.** `@JdbcTest` is `@Transactional`: each test method runs
33	inside a transaction that Spring rolls back when the method ends. Rows a test inserts disappear
34	afterward, so tests can't affect each other and no cleanup code is needed.
35	
36	**Spring: which database?** `@JdbcTest` can replace the application's `DataSource` with an
37	embedded in-memory database. By default (Spring Boot 3.4+) it doesn't replace one that was set
38	up for tests. Ours comes from `@ServiceConnection` in `TestcontainersConfiguration`, so the tests
39	run against real Postgres. Different test annotations mean a different cached context, so this
40	class gets its own container (see
41	[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).
42	
43	**Kotlin: `@Autowired constructor(...)`.** Annotating the primary constructor requires writing
44	the `constructor` keyword. Normally it's left out. In the main code, Spring creates beans and
45	calls their single constructor automatically. Test classes are created by **JUnit**, and
46	Spring's JUnit extension only fills constructor parameters when the constructor is marked
47	`@Autowired`. The `val` parameters make the injected objects read-only properties, the same as in
48	[InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md). The trailing comma is
49	the same as in [InventoryItem.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md).
50	
51	**Kotlin: `@Import(A::class, B::class)`.** `@Import`'s parameter is an array, and Kotlin
52	passes several values as varargs.
53	
54	### A test helper
55	
56	```kotlin
57	private fun insert(skuId: String, quantity: Int) {
58	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)")
59	        .params(skuId, quantity)
60	        .update()
61	}
62	```
63	
64	**Why insert with SQL instead of going through the app:** there's no "add stock" endpoint yet.
65	Even once there is, a test that controls exactly which rows exist is clearer, and it doesn't
66	fail because of a bug in some other feature. This is the test *seeding* we talked about.
67	
68	**Spring:** `?` are positional parameters. `.params(...)` binds them in order. The values are
69	sent to Postgres separately from the SQL text, so there's no SQL injection risk. `.update()` runs
70	the statement and returns the number of rows affected (ignored here).
71	
72	**Kotlin:** `private` functions need no KDoc under the project standard. JUnit ignores it
73	because it has no `@Test`.
74	
75	### Empty table
76	
77	```kotlin
78	/** No rows means an empty list, never null. */
79	@Test
80	fun `findAll returns an empty list when there are no SKUs`() {
81	    assertTrue(inventoryRepository.findAll().isEmpty())
82	}
83	```
84	
85	**Kotlin: backtick names.** A function name in backticks can contain spaces, so a test reads
86	as a sentence, and JUnit reports it that way. This is only for tests. The JVM still forbids some
87	characters in names, such as `.`, `:`, `/` and `<`.
88	
89	**Kotlin: `kotlin.test` assertions.** `assertTrue`, `assertEquals` and `assertFailsWith` come
90	from `kotlin-test` (the `kotlin-test-junit5` dependency), a thin Kotlin layer over JUnit's
91	assertions.
92	
93	**Contract:** "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array."
94	
95	### Mapping and order
96	
97	```kotlin
98	@Test
99	fun `findAll returns every SKU ordered by SKU id`() {
100	    insert("widget", 5)
101	    insert("CW-XYCS-BM-01", 10)
102	    insert("gadget", 3)
103	
104	    assertEquals(
105	        listOf(
106	            InventoryItem("CW-XYCS-BM-01", 10),
107	            InventoryItem("gadget", 3),
108	            InventoryItem("widget", 5),
109	        ),
110	        inventoryRepository.findAll(),
111	    )
112	}
113	```
114	
115	**Why the rows are inserted out of order:** if they were inserted in the expected order, the
116	test could pass even without `ORDER BY`, because Postgres often returns rows in insertion order.
117	
118	**Kotlin: `listOf(...)`** creates a read-only `List`. `assertEquals(expected, actual)` (expected
119	first) compares the lists element by element with `equals`. That only works because
120	`InventoryItem` is a `data class`. With a plain class, two items with the same values would not
121	be equal (see [InventoryItem.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md)).
122	
123	### Zero stock is listed
124	
125	```kotlin
126	@Test
127	fun `findAll includes SKUs with zero stock`() {
128	    insert("sold-out", 0)
129	
130	    assertEquals(listOf(InventoryItem("sold-out", 0)), inventoryRepository.findAll())
131	}
132	```
133	
134	**Why:** it pins the 2026-09-24 decision. A sold-out SKU still exists and is listed. If
135	someone later adds `WHERE quantity > 0`, this test fails.
136	
137	### The database backstop
138	
139	```kotlin
140	@Test
141	fun `database rejects an update that would make quantity negative`() {
142	    insert("widget", 1)
143	
144	    assertFailsWith<DataIntegrityViolationException> {
145	        jdbcClient.sql("UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 2 WHERE sku_id = ?")
146	            .param("widget")
147	            .update()
148	    }
149	}
150	```
151	
152	**Why this bypasses the repository:** the point is to show what happens if application code
153	is wrong. The `UPDATE` deliberately has no `quantity >= ?` guard, so the only thing stopping it
154	is the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint from
155	[V1__create_inventory.sql](../../main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md).
156	
157	**Kotlin: `assertFailsWith<T> { ... }`.** It runs the lambda and passes only if the lambda throws
158	a `T`. It returns the exception if you want to inspect it. `T` is a reified type parameter (see
159	[InventoryApplication.kt](../../main/InventoryApplication.kt.md)), which is how the function can
160	check the exception type at runtime. JUnit's version is `assertThrows(X.class, () -> ...)`.
161	
162	**Spring:** Postgres answers with SQLSTATE `23514` (check violation). Spring's exception
163	translation maps it to `DataIntegrityViolationException`, a database-independent exception, so
164	the test doesn't depend on Postgres error codes.
165	
166	The failed statement aborts the test's transaction in Postgres, and the rollback at the end of
167	the test discards everything anyway.
168	
169	## Check your understanding
170	
171	- Why does `InventoryRepository::class` have to be in `@Import` here, but not in
172	  `InventoryControllerTest`?
173	- If `@JdbcTest` didn't roll back, which test here would start failing, and when?
174	- What would the ordering test prove if the rows were inserted already sorted?

39	run against real Postgres. Different test annotations mean a different cached context, so this
40	class gets its own container (see
41	[TestcontainersConfiguration.kt](../support/TestcontainersConfiguration.kt.md)).
42	
43	**Kotlin: `@Autowired constructor(...)`.** Annotating the primary constructor requires writing
44	the `constructor` keyword. Normally it's left out. In the main code, Spring creates beans and
45	calls their single constructor automatically. Test classes are created by **JUnit**, and
46	Spring's JUnit extension only fills constructor parameters when the constructor is marked
47	`@Autowired`. The `val` parameters make the injected objects read-only properties, the same as in
48	[InventoryRepository.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryRepository.kt.md). The trailing comma is
49	the same as in [InventoryItem.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md).
50	
51	**Kotlin: `@Import(A::class, B::class)`.** `@Import`'s parameter is an array, and Kotlin
52	passes several values as varargs.
53	
54	### A test helper
55	
56	```kotlin
57	private fun insert(skuId: String, quantity: Int) {
58	    jdbcClient.sql("INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)")
59	        .params(skuId, quantity)
60	        .update()
61	}
62	```
63	
64	**Why insert with SQL instead of going through the app:** there's no "add stock" endpoint yet.
65	Even once there is, a test that controls exactly which rows exist is clearer, and it doesn't
66	fail because of a bug in some other feature. This is the test *seeding* we talked about.
67	
68	**Spring:** `?` are positional parameters. `.params(...)` binds them in order. The values are
69	sent to Postgres separately from the SQL text, so there's no SQL injection risk. `.update()` runs
70	the statement and returns the number of rows affected (ignored here).
71	
72	**Kotlin:** `private` functions need no KDoc under the project standard. JUnit ignores it
73	because it has no `@Test`.
74	
75	### Empty table
76	
77	```kotlin
78	/** No rows means an empty list, never null. */
79	@Test
80	fun `findAll returns an empty list when there are no SKUs`() {
81	    assertTrue(inventoryRepository.findAll().isEmpty())
82	}
83	```
84	
85	**Kotlin: backtick names.** A function name in backticks can contain spaces, so a test reads
86	as a sentence, and JUnit reports it that way. This is only for tests. The JVM still forbids some
87	characters in names, such as `.`, `:`, `/` and `<`.
88	
89	**Kotlin: `kotlin.test` assertions.** `assertTrue`, `assertEquals` and `assertFailsWith` come
90	from `kotlin-test` (the `kotlin-test-junit5` dependency), a thin Kotlin layer over JUnit's
91	assertions.
92	
93	**Contract:** "If no SKUs exist, returns an empty array."
94	
95	### Mapping and order
96	
97	```kotlin
98	@Test
99	fun `findAll returns every SKU ordered by SKU id`() {
100	    insert("widget", 5)
101	    insert("CW-XYCS-BM-01", 10)
102	    insert("gadget", 3)
103	
104	    assertEquals(
105	        listOf(
106	            InventoryItem("CW-XYCS-BM-01", 10),
107	            InventoryItem("gadget", 3),
108	            InventoryItem("widget", 5),
109	        ),
110	        inventoryRepository.findAll(),
111	    )
112	}
113	```
114	
115	**Why the rows are inserted out of order:** if they were inserted in the expected order, the
116	test could pass even without `ORDER BY`, because Postgres often returns rows in insertion order.
117	
118	**Kotlin: `listOf(...)`** creates a read-only `List`. `assertEquals(expected, actual)` (expected
119	first) compares the lists element by element with `equals`. That only works because
120	`InventoryItem` is a `data class`. With a plain class, two items with the same values would not
121	be equal (see [InventoryItem.kt](../../main/inventory/InventoryItem.kt.md)).
122	
123	### Zero stock is listed
124	
125	```kotlin
126	@Test
127	fun `findAll includes SKUs with zero stock`() {
128	    insert("sold-out", 0)
129	
130	    assertEquals(listOf(InventoryItem("sold-out", 0)), inventoryRepository.findAll())
131	}
132	```
133	
134	**Why:** it pins the 2026-09-24 decision. A sold-out SKU still exists and is listed. If
135	someone later adds `WHERE quantity > 0`, this test fails.
136	
137	### The database backstop
138	
139	```kotlin
140	@Test
141	fun `database rejects an update that would make quantity negative`() {
142	    insert("widget", 1)
143	
144	    assertFailsWith<DataIntegrityViolationException> {
145	        jdbcClient.sql("UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 2 WHERE sku_id = ?")
146	            .param("widget")
147	            .update()
148	    }
149	}
150	```
151	
152	**Why this bypasses the repository:** the point is to show what happens if application code
153	is wrong. The `UPDATE` deliberately has no `quantity >= ?` guard, so the only thing stopping it
154	is the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint from
155	[V1__create_inventory.sql](../../main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql.md).
156	
157	**Kotlin: `assertFailsWith<T> { ... }`.** It runs the lambda and passes only if the lambda throws
158	a `T`. It returns the exception if you want to inspect it. `T` is a reified type parameter (see
159	[InventoryApplication.kt](../../main/InventoryApplication.kt.md)), which is how the function can
160	check the exception type at runtime. JUnit's version is `assertThrows(X.class, () -> ...)`.
161	
162	**Spring:** Postgres answers with SQLSTATE `23514` (check violation). Spring's exception
163	translation maps it to `DataIntegrityViolationException`, a database-independent exception, so
164	the test doesn't depend on Postgres error codes.
165	
166	The failed statement aborts the test's transaction in Postgres, and the rollback at the end of
167	the test discards everything anyway.
168	
169	## Check your understanding
170	
171	- Why does `InventoryRepository::class` have to be in `@Import` here, but not in
172	  `InventoryControllerTest`?
173	- If `@JdbcTest` didn't roll back, which test here would start failing, and when?
174	- What would the ordering test prove if the rows were inserted already sorted?

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

`GET /inventory` is built and tested, and `/sync-docs` is finished. Nothing is committed yet.

**What was built:**
- **Migration** `V1__create_inventory.sql`: the `inventory` table, with `sku_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY` and `quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0)`.
- **Code** in the `inventory` package: `InventoryItem` (data class) → `InventoryRepository.findAll()` (`JdbcClient`, `ORDER BY sku_id`) → `InventoryService` (a pass-through for now) → `InventoryController` (`@GetMapping`).
- **Tests:** 6 new tests, 7 in total, all passing.
  - `InventoryRepositoryTest` (4 tests against real Postgres): empty table, mapping and order, zero-stock rows, and the `CHECK` constraint rejecting negative stock. That last one is the "Database backstop" item from the oversell test plan, now checked off.
  - `InventoryControllerTest` (2 tests through the full stack with MockMvc): an empty `[]`, and the exact JSON with strict matching.
  - The first build failed only because Docker Desktop wasn't running. I started it and every test passed.
- **Running app:** I started it with `bootRun`, and `curl /inventory` returned `200`, `application/json`, `[]`. Flyway applied V1 on startup.

**Docs:**
- Seven new study-notes files, 22 new rows in the concepts index, and two outdated lines fixed in the scaffold notes.
- **README:** the endpoint is marked Done, with a curl example. Your three decisions are recorded, and demo seed data is listed as an open decision.
- **TODO:** updated, including a new item for the contract-validation test.

**What the reviewer caught:**
1. My code comment and notes said the reflection alternative was `DataClassRowMapper`. `JdbcClient` actually uses `SimplePropertyRowMapper`. The reviewer checked the Spring source, and I fixed both places.
2. The controller notes said that without `@ResponseBody` any return value is treated as a view name. That's only true for a `String`. A `List` becomes model data for a view named after the URL, and since no such view exists, the request fails. This mattered because one of your self-check questions depends on it.
3. Smaller fixes:
   - `STRICT` JSON comparison doesn't check number types; it treats `10` and `10.0` as equal.
   - The `@Autowired`-constructor rule for tests only holds with default settings.
   - Two YAML blocks in the notes are now labelled as abridged from the contract.
   - A paragraph was moved to the right section.
   - Added a "public by default" Kotlin point to the notes and the concepts index.

**Tooling issue:** `scripts/check_notes.py` hangs when run by hand from a shell that isn't a terminal. It reads any such stdin as hook input and waits for data. The hooks themselves are unaffected. I added it to TODO with a workaround (`< /dev/null`).

Use after every feature, or when Robert asks to go through or explain code.
argument-hint: "[optional: files, commit range, or topic; defaults to everything since the last walkthrough]"
---

# /walkthrough $ARGUMENTS

Robert is learning Kotlin through this project. He has to understand the code well
enough to explain and defend it in an interview. Go at his pace. This is a
conversation, not a lecture.

## 1. Establish scope

- If `$ARGUMENTS` names files, a commit range or a topic, use that.
- Otherwise, find the last walkthrough log in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/` and read the
  commit SHA it records. The scope is `<that sha>..HEAD` plus any uncommitted changes.
  If there are no logs yet, the scope is everything under `src/` plus the build files.

Show the list of files in scope. Order them along the path a request takes:
build/config → entry point → controller → service → repository/model → error handling → tests.
Ask whether that order works for him before starting.

## 2. Walk through one file at a time

Each source file has a study-notes file in `docs/learning/notes/` (mapping in its README).
Read the source and its notes first, and use the notes as your script: they hold the
explanations and the check-your-understanding questions. If the notes are missing or don't
match the code, run `/sync-docs` before starting.

For each file:

1. **Role.** One or two sentences on what this file is for and how a request reaches it.
2. **Code in small chunks** (roughly 5–20 lines), following the notes' sections. Quote each chunk with its `path:line` reference, then explain:
   - every Kotlin feature in it: what it does, why it's idiomatic, and what the Java
     equivalent would look like when that comparison helps;
   - any Spring behavior that isn't visible in the code (what the framework does with the
     annotation, when the object is created, what runs before and after);
   - the design decision, and the alternative we rejected and why.
3. **Pause.** Ask whether he has questions about the file. Then ask one short
   check-your-understanding question, for example: "What happens if `quantity` is 0 here?"
   or "Why is this a `val`?" or "What would the response be if the SKU doesn't exist?"
   **Wait for his reply before moving to the next file.** Don't answer your own question.
4. If his answer is wrong or partial, re-explain it another way. Don't just repeat the
   explanation.
5. If a question shows that a note or code comment is unclear or wrong, offer to fix it. Add
   anything new you had to explain to the file's notes, so the notes improve after every walkthrough.

Where a quick experiment would help, suggest one he can run himself, such as changing a
value and rerunning a test to watch it fail, or a `curl` call against the running app.

## 3. Wrap up

- Recap the concepts covered in 3–6 bullets.
- Ask whether anything should be revisited.

## 4. Log it

Write `docs/learning/walkthroughs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<short-slug>.md` containing:

```
# Walkthrough: <feature/topic>
- Date: <date>
- Covers: <first sha>..<HEAD sha> (plus uncommitted: yes/no)
- Files: <list>

## Concepts covered
- <concept>: <one-line summary in Robert's terms>

## Questions Robert asked
- Q: ... / A: ...

## Understanding checks
- <question> → <how he answered, what was clarified>

## Follow-ups
- <comments to fix, topics to revisit, exercises to try>
```

Then update `docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md`. For each concept seen for the first time, add a
row with the concept, a short explanation, and a `path:line` link to where it first appears in
this codebase. Don't add duplicate rows.
----

Give a short plan covering the files to create or change, each one's layer (controller / service /

  Java-style Kotlin.

Run the Gradle build and tests (`./gradlew build` or `gradlew.bat build`). Report the result
truthfully. If something fails, fix it and explain the failure. The failure is often
the most useful thing to learn from.

Run `/sync-docs`. It writes or updates the study notes for every changed file, the concepts
index, the README (endpoint status, curl examples, decision records) and the TODO, then runs
the `doc-reviewer` agent until it returns `PASS`. Tell Robert what the reviewer caught.

`python scripts/check_notes.py` must print nothing. (The Stop hook enforces this too.)

attribution line from the system reminder), and commit only if Robert says so. Finish with:
"Ready for `/walkthrough`, then `/ship`." Do not start another feature in this turn.

# CLAUDE.md

Project memory for Claude Code. Loaded automatically at the start of every session.

## What this project is

A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
code must work and come with study notes that teach it. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the
follow-up interview?" as a requirement alongside passing the tests.

## Source of truth

- **API contract:** [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml). Paths, status codes,
  content types and schemas must match it exactly. Error responses (400/404) are
  `text/plain` strings, not JSON. `quantity` in requests has `minimum: 1`.
- If the contract is ambiguous (e.g. malformed JSON, missing body, SKU id format),
  stop and ask Robert rather than guessing; record the decision in the README.

## Task list

[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) is the working task list. Read it at the start of each session,
check items off as they are done, and add new items as they come up. Its **oversell protection
test plan** is a hard requirement: a purchase must never oversell, even under concurrent requests.
Every feature that touches stock must add or extend tests from that plan.

## Stack

- Kotlin on the JVM, Spring Boot (Spring MVC), Gradle with the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`).
  Chosen because it is what Nuuly runs in production.
- PostgreSQL (run with Docker Compose; Testcontainers in tests). Stock changes are single atomic
  SQL statements, backed by `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`. See the README decision record.
- Tests: JUnit Jupiter 6 (Spring Boot 4's version; same API as JUnit 5) with Spring's test support.
- Open decisions are tracked in the README under "Open decisions". Do not settle
  one silently; propose it, explain the trade-offs, and let Robert choose.

## Documentation standard: clean code + study notes

The code reads like good production code. The teaching lives in a **study-notes file per
source file** under [docs/learning/notes/](docs/learning/notes/README.md) (the README there
has the path mapping and format).

**In the code:**

1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.
   Keep it short: what it does and where it sits in the request flow
   (controller → service → repository). Use `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` only when
   they add information. Test classes get a KDoc saying what they cover.
   A PostToolUse hook ([scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py)) enforces this mechanically.
2. **Inline comments only for decisions and contract rules**, one or two lines each:
   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
3. **First line links to the notes**: `// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`
   (`#` in YAML, `--` in SQL). `check_notes.py` verifies it.
4. **No teaching comments in code**: no `// Kotlin:` / `// Spring:` explanations, and no narration.
   Build files and `application.yml` may carry a one-line "what it's for" where it isn't obvious.

**In the notes** (`docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`):

1. Walk the file top to bottom in small chunks. **Quote each chunk** (don't reference line numbers)
   and explain it under `**Kotlin:**` (language features, with the Java equivalent when that
   helps), `**Spring:**` (framework behavior the code doesn't show), `**Why:**` and `**Contract:**`.
2. Explain a concept in full in the first notes file where it appears; elsewhere, link back to it.
   Index new concepts in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
3. End with "Check your understanding" questions, without answers.

**Keeping them in sync:** every code change updates its notes in the same piece of work. Run
`/sync-docs` to update them. A `Stop` hook ([scripts/check_notes.py](scripts/check_notes.py)) keeps
Claude working while any source file has changed more recently than its notes (or has none).

## Feature workflow

Use `/feature <description>` for any new behavior. It runs the whole loop:
contract check → plan (Robert approves) → tests + implementation → build →
`/sync-docs` (notes, concepts index, README, TODO, then the `doc-reviewer` agent) → hand-off to `/walkthrough`.
For any other code change, run `/sync-docs` before handing the work back.

- **Do not start the next feature until the walkthrough for the current one is done.**
- After the walkthrough, fix any note or comment that turned out to be unclear.
- Keep changes small and commit-sized. The reviewers want a readable, unsquashed
  git history. Propose a commit message, but only commit when Robert says so or runs `/ship`.

## Git workflow: never work on main

- **Every session starts on a new branch.** If the session starts on `main`, ask Robert what the
  session's work is before touching anything, then run
  `git switch main && git pull --ff-only && git switch -c <type>/<slug>`, where `<type>` is
  `feature`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs` or `test` (e.g. `feature/get-inventory`).
- One branch per piece of work. Commit in small, logical steps; the reviewers read the history.
- **`/ship`** is the only way work reaches `main`: push → PR → merge commit → back to an
  updated `main`. Never squash or rebase merges (the brief says "Do not squash commits").
- Enforced by `scripts/branch_guard.py`:
  - a `SessionStart` hook flags when the session starts on `main`
  - a `PreToolUse` hook blocks, while on `main`, edits to repo files and `git commit`/`git push`
  - on any branch, it blocks pushes to `main` and squash/rebase merges

## Project tooling (.claude/)

- `skills/feature/`: the `/feature` workflow above.
- `skills/walkthrough/`: `/walkthrough`, an interactive line-by-line teaching session
  on recent changes, logged to [docs/learning/walkthroughs/](docs/learning/walkthroughs/).
- `skills/ship/`: `/ship`, which pushes the current branch, opens a PR, and merges it into
  `main` with a merge commit. Build, test and review gates will be added later.

stderr and exits 2. Claude Code then keeps Claude working with that message as feedback, and
Claude runs /sync-docs. It also reports notes whose source file no longer exists.

already sent Claude back to work (`stop_hook_active`), the script lets the turn end.

(exit 1 when something is stale).

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

    ("", "", lambda p: "/" not in p and (p.endswith(".gradle.kts") or p == "compose.yaml")),
]

    """Map a repo-relative source path to its notes path, or None if it needs no notes."""
    for src_prefix, notes_prefix, is_source in MAPPINGS:
        if source.startswith(src_prefix):

    return problems

            payload = json.load(sys.stdin)

# CLAUDE.md

Project memory for Claude Code. Loaded automatically at the start of every session.

## What this project is

A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).

**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
code must work and come with study notes that teach it. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the
follow-up interview?" as a requirement alongside passing the tests.

## Who writes what: Robert codes, Claude coaches

**Robert writes all production code**: everything under `src/main/` (Kotlin, SQL migrations,
`application.yml`), KDoc and `// Why:` / `// Contract:` comments included. He is learning Kotlin
by writing it, so Claude does **not** write or edit files under `src/main/`, even when that would
be faster, and even inside `/feature`.

Claude's job:

- **Tests first.** Claude writes the tests under `src/test/` before Robert starts: one or more
  per acceptance criterion. They are the spec, and they fail until his code is right.
- **Coach, don't solve.** Explain the concepts he needs, point to the file and layer to work
  in, and answer questions. When he's stuck, give hints in increasing order: the concept, then
  the API or annotation to look at, then the shape of the code in words. Show actual code only
  when he asks for it, and then as a snippet in chat for him to type, never as a file edit.
- **Review his code** when he asks: correctness against the contract and tests, idiomatic Kotlin,
  and the documentation standard. Explain each suggestion; he makes the change.
- **Everything around the code:** tests, study notes, README, TODO, build runs and tooling.

Exception: Claude may edit `src/main/` only when Robert explicitly asks for that specific edit
in the current conversation. The `GET /inventory` code was written by Claude before this rule
existed (2026-09-24).

## Source of truth

- **API contract:** [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml). Paths, status codes,
  content types and schemas must match it exactly. Error responses (400/404) are
  `text/plain` strings, not JSON. `quantity` in requests has `minimum: 1`.
- If the contract is ambiguous (e.g. malformed JSON, missing body, SKU id format),
  stop and ask Robert rather than guessing; record the decision in the README.

## Task list

[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) is the working task list. Read it at the start of each session,
check items off as they are done, and add new items as they come up. Its **oversell protection
test plan** is a hard requirement: a purchase must never oversell, even under concurrent requests.
Every feature that touches stock must add or extend tests from that plan.

## Stack

- Kotlin on the JVM, Spring Boot (Spring MVC), Gradle with the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`).
  Chosen because it is what Nuuly runs in production.
- PostgreSQL (run with Docker Compose; Testcontainers in tests). Stock changes are single atomic
  SQL statements, backed by `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`. See the README decision record.
- Tests: JUnit Jupiter 6 (Spring Boot 4's version; same API as JUnit 5) with Spring's test support.
- Open decisions are tracked in the README under "Open decisions". Do not settle
  one silently; propose it, explain the trade-offs, and let Robert choose.

## Documentation standard: clean code + study notes

The code reads like good production code. The teaching lives in a **study-notes file per
source file** under [docs/learning/notes/](docs/learning/notes/README.md) (the README there
has the path mapping and format).

**In the code:**

1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.
   Keep it short: what it does and where it sits in the request flow
   (controller → service → repository). Use `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` only when
   they add information. Test classes get a KDoc saying what they cover.
   A PostToolUse hook ([scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py)) enforces this mechanically.
2. **Inline comments only for decisions and contract rules**, one or two lines each:
   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
3. **First line links to the notes**: `// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`
   (`#` in YAML, `--` in SQL). `check_notes.py` verifies it.
4. **No teaching comments in code**: no `// Kotlin:` / `// Spring:` explanations, and no narration.
   Build files and `application.yml` may carry a one-line "what it's for" where it isn't obvious.

**In the notes** (`docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`):

1. Walk the file top to bottom in small chunks. **Quote each chunk** (don't reference line numbers)
   and explain it under `**Kotlin:**` (language features, with the Java equivalent when that
   helps), `**Spring:**` (framework behavior the code doesn't show), `**Why:**` and `**Contract:**`.
2. Explain a concept in full in the first notes file where it appears; elsewhere, link back to it.
   Index new concepts in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
3. End with "Check your understanding" questions, without answers.

**Keeping them in sync:** every code change updates its notes in the same piece of work. Run
`/sync-docs` to update them. A `Stop` hook ([scripts/check_notes.py](scripts/check_notes.py)) keeps
Claude working while any source file has changed more recently than its notes (or has none).

## Feature workflow

Use `/feature <description>` for any new behavior. It runs the whole loop:
contract check → plan (Robert approves) → tests + implementation → build →
`/sync-docs` (notes, concepts index, README, TODO, then the `doc-reviewer` agent) → hand-off to `/walkthrough`.
For any other code change, run `/sync-docs` before handing the work back.

- **Do not start the next feature until the walkthrough for the current one is done.**
- After the walkthrough, fix any note or comment that turned out to be unclear.
- Keep changes small and commit-sized. The reviewers want a readable, unsquashed
  git history. Propose a commit message, but only commit when Robert says so or runs `/ship`.

## Git workflow: never work on main

- **Every session starts on a new branch.** If the session starts on `main`, ask Robert what the
  session's work is before touching anything, then run
  `git switch main && git pull --ff-only && git switch -c <type>/<slug>`, where `<type>` is
  `feature`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs` or `test` (e.g. `feature/get-inventory`).
- One branch per piece of work. Commit in small, logical steps; the reviewers read the history.
- **`/ship`** is the only way work reaches `main`: push → PR → merge commit → back to an
  updated `main`. Never squash or rebase merges (the brief says "Do not squash commits").
- Enforced by `scripts/branch_guard.py`:
  - a `SessionStart` hook flags when the session starts on `main`
  - a `PreToolUse` hook blocks, while on `main`, edits to repo files and `git commit`/`git push`
  - on any branch, it blocks pushes to `main` and squash/rebase merges

## Project tooling (.claude/)

- `skills/feature/`: the `/feature` workflow above.
- `skills/walkthrough/`: `/walkthrough`, an interactive line-by-line teaching session
  on recent changes, logged to [docs/learning/walkthroughs/](docs/learning/walkthroughs/).
- `skills/ship/`: `/ship`, which pushes the current branch, opens a PR, and merges it into
  `main` with a merge commit. Build, test and review gates will be added later.
- `skills/sync-docs/`: `/sync-docs`, which updates study notes, the concepts index, the README
  and TODO for whatever code changed, then runs `doc-reviewer`.
- `agents/doc-reviewer.md`: read-only reviewer that checks changed code and its notes against
  the documentation standard above, accuracy first.
- `TODO.md`: the working task list.
- `settings.json` hooks:
  - `SessionStart` + `PreToolUse`: `scripts/branch_guard.py` (see Git workflow).
  - `Stop`: exports session transcripts to [docs/ai-sessions/](docs/ai-sessions/), and runs
    `scripts/check_notes.py` (stale or missing study notes send Claude back to `/sync-docs`).
  - `PostToolUse` (Edit/Write): runs `scripts/check_kdoc.py` on edited `.kt` files and
    reports missing KDoc back to Claude.

## Environment

Windows 11. Claude has PowerShell and Git Bash available. Python is on PATH and is
used for the hook scripts.

# /feature: $ARGUMENTS

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip one because the feature looks small.

## 0. Gate: previous walkthrough done?

Check the newest file in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/`. If there are commits touching
`src/` after the commit it records, a walkthrough is still owed. Tell Robert and suggest
running `/walkthrough` first. Continue only if he says to.

## 1. Pin the behavior to the contract

Read `src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` and quote the exact part this feature implements.
List the acceptance criteria as a checklist: method + path, request schema and validation,
every response status with its content type (`application/json` vs `text/plain`), and body shape.
List any ambiguity the contract leaves open and ask Robert how to resolve it.

## 2. Plan, then wait for approval

Give a short plan covering the files to create or change, each one's layer (controller / service /
repository / model / config / test), and the Kotlin and Spring concepts this feature will
introduce for the first time. That list becomes the agenda for the walkthrough.
**Stop and wait for Robert to approve the plan.**

## 3. Tests and implementation

- Write the tests alongside the code: at least one per acceptance criterion, covering the error
  paths as well as the happy path.
- Follow the documentation standard in `CLAUDE.md`: short KDoc, one-line `// Why:` and
  `// Contract:` comments, and no teaching comments in code. Prefer idiomatic Kotlin; when an
  idiom is dense, keep it and explain it in the file's study notes rather than writing
  Java-style Kotlin.
- The PostToolUse hook reports missing KDoc after each edit. Fix those gaps immediately.

## 4. Build and test

Run the Gradle build and tests (`./gradlew build` or `gradlew.bat build`). Report the result
truthfully. If something fails, fix it and explain the failure. The failure is often
the most useful thing to learn from.

## 5. Documentation

Run `/sync-docs`. It writes or updates the study notes for every changed file, the concepts
index, the README (endpoint status, curl examples, decision records) and the TODO, then runs
the `doc-reviewer` agent until it returns `PASS`. Tell Robert what the reviewer caught.

## 6. Check the docs gate

`python scripts/check_notes.py` must print nothing. (The Stop hook enforces this too.)

## 7. Hand-off

Summarize what was built. Propose a commit message (small and descriptive, ending with the
attribution line from the system reminder), and commit only if Robert says so. Finish with:
"Ready for `/walkthrough`, then `/ship`." Do not start another feature in this turn.

input.new_string:
Give a short plan covering:

- the files Robert will create or change, each one's layer (controller / service / repository /
  model / migration), and what each needs to do, described in words and signatures, not code;
- the test files you will write, and which acceptance criterion each test covers;
- the Kotlin and Spring concepts this feature introduces for the first time. That list is both
  what you'll coach him through and the agenda for the walkthrough.

**Stop and wait for Robert to approve the plan.**

## 3. Write the failing tests

- Write the tests under `src/test/` first: at least one per acceptance criterion, covering the
  error paths as well as the happy path. They are the spec for Robert's code.
- Tests reference the classes and functions named in the plan. The build won't compile until he
  creates them; that's expected. Tell him which compile errors and failures to expect.
- Follow the documentation standard in `CLAUDE.md` for the test files (KDoc, `// Why:`, notes
  header line).

## 4. Robert writes the code; you coach

- Hand over a short checklist: which file to write next and what it must do, in request-path
  order (usually migration → model → repository → service → controller). Suggest a first
  test to make pass.
- **Hints go in increasing order**: the concept → the API or annotation to look up → the shape
  of the code in words → a code snippet, but only when he asks, and in chat for him to type.
  Never write the file for him.
- Explain concepts when he asks or when you see him stuck on one, with the Java equivalent
  when that helps.
- Run the build (`gradlew.bat build`) when he asks, and explain failures in terms of what his
  code does. Report results truthfully.
- The KDoc hook only runs on your edits, so remind him that every non-private declaration he
  writes needs KDoc, plus the `// Study notes:` header line.
- While his code is in progress, its study notes are expected to lag. Don't write notes for
  half-finished code.

## 4b. Review

When the tests pass, review his code: contract conformance, idiomatic Kotlin (flag
Java-style Kotlin and explain the idiom), the documentation standard, and anything the tests
don't catch. Explain each point; he makes the changes. Rerun the build after his fixes.

# /feature: $ARGUMENTS

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip one because the feature looks small.

**Robert writes the production code; you coach.** Never create or edit files under `src/main/`
unless Robert explicitly asks for that specific edit (see "Who writes what" in `CLAUDE.md`).
Your deliverables are the contract check, the plan, the tests, hints, reviews and the docs.

## 0. Gate: previous walkthrough done?

Check the newest file in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/`. If there are commits touching
`src/` after the commit it records, a walkthrough is still owed. Tell Robert and suggest
running `/walkthrough` first. Continue only if he says to.

## 1. Pin the behavior to the contract

Read `src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml` and quote the exact part this feature implements.
List the acceptance criteria as a checklist: method + path, request schema and validation,
every response status with its content type (`application/json` vs `text/plain`), and body shape.
List any ambiguity the contract leaves open and ask Robert how to resolve it.

## 2. Plan, then wait for approval

Give a short plan covering:

- the files Robert will create or change, each one's layer (controller / service / repository /
  model / migration), and what each needs to do, described in words and signatures, not code;
- the test files you will write, and which acceptance criterion each test covers;
- the Kotlin and Spring concepts this feature introduces for the first time. That list is both
  what you'll coach him through and the agenda for the walkthrough.

**Stop and wait for Robert to approve the plan.**

## 3. Write the failing tests

- Write the tests under `src/test/` first: at least one per acceptance criterion, covering the
  error paths as well as the happy path. They are the spec for Robert's code.
- Tests reference the classes and functions named in the plan. The build won't compile until he
  creates them; that's expected. Tell him which compile errors and failures to expect.
- Follow the documentation standard in `CLAUDE.md` for the test files (KDoc, `// Why:`, notes
  header line).

## 4. Robert writes the code; you coach

- Hand over a short checklist: which file to write next and what it must do, in request-path
  order (usually migration → model → repository → service → controller). Suggest a first
  test to make pass.
- **Hints go in increasing order**: the concept → the API or annotation to look up → the shape
  of the code in words → a code snippet, but only when he asks, and in chat for him to type.
  Never write the file for him.
- Explain concepts when he asks or when you see him stuck on one, with the Java equivalent
  when that helps.
- Run the build (`gradlew.bat build`) when he asks, and explain failures in terms of what his
  code does. Report results truthfully.
- The KDoc hook only runs on your edits, so remind him that every non-private declaration he
  writes needs KDoc, plus the `// Study notes:` header line.
- While his code is in progress, its study notes are expected to lag. Don't write notes for
  half-finished code.

## 4b. Review

When the tests pass, review his code: contract conformance, idiomatic Kotlin (flag
Java-style Kotlin and explain the idiom), the documentation standard, and anything the tests
don't catch. Explain each point; he makes the changes. Rerun the build after his fixes.

## 5. Documentation

Once the build is green and the review is done, run `/sync-docs`. It writes or updates the
study notes for every changed file (describing the code Robert wrote), the concepts
index, the README (endpoint status, curl examples, decision records) and the TODO, then runs
the `doc-reviewer` agent until it returns `PASS`. Tell Robert what the reviewer caught.

## 6. Check the docs gate

`python scripts/check_notes.py` must print nothing. (The Stop hook enforces this too.)

## 7. Hand-off

Summarize what was built. Propose a commit message (small and descriptive, ending with the
attribution line from the system reminder), and commit only if Robert says so. Finish with:
"Ready for `/walkthrough`, then `/ship`." Do not start another feature in this turn.

---
name: walkthrough
description: Interactive teaching session that walks Robert through recently written code line by line, explaining Kotlin and Spring concepts, pausing for questions and checking understanding, then logs the session to docs/learning. Use after every feature, or when Robert asks to go through or explain code.
argument-hint: "[optional: files, commit range, or topic; defaults to everything since the last walkthrough]"
---

# /walkthrough $ARGUMENTS

Robert is learning Kotlin through this project. He has to understand the code well
enough to explain and defend it in an interview. Go at his pace. This is a
conversation, not a lecture.

## 1. Establish scope

- If `$ARGUMENTS` names files, a commit range or a topic, use that.
- Otherwise, find the last walkthrough log in `docs/learning/walkthroughs/` and read the
  commit SHA it records. The scope is `<that sha>..HEAD` plus any uncommitted changes.
  If there are no logs yet, the scope is everything under `src/` plus the build files.

Show the list of files in scope. Order them along the path a request takes:
build/config → entry point → controller → service → repository/model → error handling → tests.
Ask whether that order works for him before starting.

## 2. Walk through one file at a time

Each source file has a study-notes file in `docs/learning/notes/` (mapping in its README).
Read the source and its notes first, and use the notes as your script: they hold the
explanations and the check-your-understanding questions. If the notes are missing or don't
match the code, run `/sync-docs` before starting.

For each file:

1. **Role.** One or two sentences on what this file is for and how a request reaches it.
2. **Code in small chunks** (roughly 5–20 lines), following the notes' sections. Quote each chunk with its `path:line` reference, then explain:
   - every Kotlin feature in it: what it does, why it's idiomatic, and what the Java
     equivalent would look like when that comparison helps;
   - any Spring behavior that isn't visible in the code (what the framework does with the
     annotation, when the object is created, what runs before and after);
   - the design decision, and the alternative we rejected and why.
3. **Pause.** Ask whether he has questions about the file. Then ask one short
   check-your-understanding question, for example: "What happens if `quantity` is 0 here?"
   or "Why is this a `val`?" or "What would the response be if the SKU doesn't exist?"
   **Wait for his reply before moving to the next file.** Don't answer your own question.
4. If his answer is wrong or partial, re-explain it another way. Don't just repeat the
   explanation.
5. If a question shows that a note or code comment is unclear or wrong, offer to fix it. Add
   anything new you had to explain to the file's notes, so the notes improve after every walkthrough.

Where a quick experiment would help, suggest one he can run himself, such as changing a
value and rerunning a test to watch it fail, or a `curl` call against the running app.

## 3. Wrap up

- Recap the concepts covered in 3–6 bullets.
- Ask whether anything should be revisited.

## 4. Log it

Write `docs/learning/walkthroughs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<short-slug>.md` containing:

```
# Walkthrough: <feature/topic>
- Date: <date>
- Covers: <first sha>..<HEAD sha> (plus uncommitted: yes/no)
- Files: <list>

## Concepts covered
- <concept>: <one-line summary in Robert's terms>

## Questions Robert asked
- Q: ... / A: ...

## Understanding checks
- <question> → <how he answered, what was clarified>

## Follow-ups
- <comments to fix, topics to revisit, exercises to try>
```

Then update `docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md`. For each concept seen for the first time, add a
row with the concept, a short explanation, and a `path:line` link to where it first appears in
this codebase. Don't add duplicate rows.

1	# Nuuly Inventory API
2	
3	A small inventory-management REST API built for the Nuuly services assessment. It
4	receives stock by SKU, processes purchases without overselling, and reports current
5	inventory levels.
6	
7	The API contract is [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml)
8	(OpenAPI 3.0.3), and the implementation must conform to it exactly. The original brief
9	is in [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).
10	
11	## Endpoints
12	
13	| Method | Path | Behavior | Responses | Status |
14	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
15	| `GET` | `/inventory` | List every SKU and its quantity (`[]` when empty) | `200` JSON array | Tests written; Robert implementing |
16	| `GET` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Current quantity for one SKU | `200` JSON, `404` text | Not started |
17	| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Add stock; creates the SKU if it is new | `200` JSON, `400` text | Not started |
18	| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}/purchase` | Deduct stock, only if enough is on hand | `200` JSON, `400` / `404` text | Not started |
19	
20	Request bodies are `{"quantity": <integer ≥ 1>}`. Success bodies are
21	`{"skuId": "...", "quantity": <integer ≥ 0>}`. Error bodies are plain-text strings
22	(`text/plain`), not JSON.
23	
24	## Tech stack
25	
26	| Choice | Why |
27	| --- | --- |
28	| **Kotlin** (JVM) | Nuuly's production language, and one I want to learn in depth (see [Learning Kotlin](#learning-kotlin-with-this-project)). |
29	| **Spring Boot**, Spring MVC | Nuuly's production framework. Nuuly evaluated Micronaut and found its speed gains didn't outweigh the environment problems it caused, so they chose Spring (see below). |
30	| **Gradle, Kotlin DSL** | The standard build for Kotlin and Spring. Build scripts are written in Kotlin too. |
31	| **PostgreSQL 18** + **Flyway** | The database enforces the no-oversell rule; Flyway applies versioned SQL migrations at startup. See the decision record below. |
32	| **JUnit 6** (Jupiter) + Spring test support | Controller tests via `MockMvc`, plus full-context integration tests. |
33	| **Testcontainers** | Tests run against a real Postgres in Docker, never an in-memory stand-in. |
34	
35	Pinned versions: **Spring Boot 4.1.1**, **Kotlin 2.3.21**, **Java 21** (Gradle toolchain),
36	**Gradle 9.7.1** (wrapper), **PostgreSQL 18**. The project was generated with Spring
37	Initializr and then trimmed by hand; the exact command is in the commit
38	"Generate the Spring Boot project with Spring Initializr".
39	
40	**Why Spring rather than Micronaut.** Seth, an architect at Nuuly, told me the team moved to
41	Spring because managing configuration across environments was painful with Micronaut. A bug in
42	that area once kept them out of production for three days. Micronaut starts faster, but for
43	long-running services a few seconds of startup matter far less than configuration that behaves
44	predictably everywhere. This project follows the same principle: the jar carries safe defaults in
45	`application.yml`, and each environment supplies its own values through environment variables or
46	command-line arguments, which Spring layers on top in a fixed order. No environment-specific
47	settings or passwords live in the repo.
48	
49	## Open decisions
50	
51	These are settled one at a time before the code that depends on them is written.
52	Each decision and its reasoning is recorded here once it is made.
53	
54	| Decision | Options under consideration | Status |
55	| --- | --- | --- |
56	| Data store | **PostgreSQL**, run with Docker Compose. Considered in-memory and H2; see below. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
57	| Concurrency on purchase | **Single atomic SQL statements** + `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` backstop. See below. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
58	| Data-access library | **`JdbcClient`**: explicit SQL, maps to immutable data classes. Considered Spring Data JDBC, Spring Data JPA, Exposed. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
59	| Controllers | **Hand-written**, plus a contract-validation test (responses checked against `inventory.yaml`). Considered generating them with `openapi-generator`, but that hides the Spring MVC wiring and is overkill for 4 endpoints. | Decided 2026-09-23 |
60	| Schema migrations | **Flyway**: versioned plain-SQL files, run automatically at startup and in tests. Considered Liquibase (XML/YAML changesets, more ceremony) and `schema.sql` (no versioning). | Decided 2026-09-23 |
61	| List order and contents | **Ordered by `sku_id`** (the contract specifies no order; a fixed one keeps responses and tests stable). **Zero-stock SKUs are listed**: a sold-out SKU still exists, and `GET /inventory/{skuId}` returns it with quantity `0`. | Decided 2026-09-24 |
62	| Column types | `sku_id TEXT` (exact, case-sensitive match for now), `quantity INTEGER` (Kotlin `Int`). Considered `BIGINT`/`Long`; overflow will be handled when adding stock instead. | Decided 2026-09-24 |
63	| Demo seed data | Tests insert their own rows. Whether a running app should start with sample data (e.g. a dev-only Flyway location) is decided once `POST /inventory/{skuId}` exists. | Open |
64	| Contract gaps | Malformed or missing JSON body, `quantity` of wrong type, SKU id format/case sensitivity (currently case-sensitive), integer overflow on add | Open |
65	
66	### Decision record: PostgreSQL and atomic SQL
67	
68	The key requirement is that **a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at
69	the same moment.** In PostgreSQL, each write is a single atomic statement, so the database
70	guarantees this without any locking code in the application:
71	
72	```sql
73	-- Receive stock: create the SKU or add to it
74	INSERT INTO inventory (sku_id, quantity) VALUES (?, ?)
75	ON CONFLICT (sku_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity = inventory.quantity + EXCLUDED.quantity
76	RETURNING sku_id, quantity;
77	
78	-- Purchase: succeeds only if enough stock exists (0 rows updated -> 404 or 400)
79	UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - ?
80	WHERE sku_id = ? AND quantity >= ?
81	RETURNING sku_id, quantity;
82	```
83	
84	There is no read-then-write race, and correctness still holds with several instances of the
85	service running. A `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint is a second line of defense.
86	
87	Alternatives we rejected:
88	
89	- **In-memory map:** needs no setup, but data is lost on restart and it only works with a
90	  single instance.
91	- **H2:** its SQL dialect differs from production databases.
92	- **Redis / document stores:** add nothing for a single integer per key.
93	
94	Kotlin doesn't favor any particular database; it uses the same JDBC drivers as Java. It does
95	favor data-access libraries that work with immutable `data class`es (`JdbcClient`, Spring Data
96	JDBC, Exposed) over JPA, which needs compiler plugins to work around Kotlin's final-by-default classes.
97	
98	The oversell guarantee is tested with several different mechanisms: race tests, a negative
99	control, multi-instance tests, load tests and property-based tests. The full plan is in
100	[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md#oversell-protection-test-plan).
101	
102	## Build and run
103	
104	**Prerequisites:** JDK 21 and Docker Desktop (running). Postgres starts automatically in a
105	container; there is nothing to install or configure by hand.
106	
107	```sh
108	./gradlew bootRun   # start the API on http://localhost:8080 (Windows: gradlew.bat bootRun)
109	./gradlew test      # run all tests, each against a throwaway Postgres container
110	./gradlew build     # compile, test and package build/libs/inventory-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
111	```
112	
113	Try it once the app is running:
114	
115	```sh
116	curl -i http://localhost:8080/inventory
117	# HTTP/1.1 200
118	# Content-Type: application/json
119	# []
120	```
121	
122	`bootRun` starts Postgres from [compose.yaml](compose.yaml) automatically (Spring Boot's
123	Docker Compose support) and stops it on shutdown. Tests don't use Compose; Testcontainers
124	starts a fresh Postgres for them. No database URL or password needs configuring.
125	
126	**Troubleshooting (Windows):** if `gradlew` says `JAVA_HOME is not set` right after installing

4	
5	## What this project is
6	
7	A take-home assessment for Nuuly: a small inventory REST API (receive stock by SKU,
8	process purchases, report inventory levels). Full brief: [docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt](docs/Nuuly_Assessment_Instructions.txt).
9	
10	**It is also a Kotlin master class.** Robert is learning Kotlin and wants to use this
11	project to learn it properly, whatever happens with the interview. Every piece of
12	code must work and come with study notes that teach it. Treat "can Robert explain every line of this in the
13	follow-up interview?" as a requirement alongside passing the tests.
14	
15	## Who writes what: Robert codes, Claude coaches
16	
17	**Robert writes all production code**: everything under `src/main/` (Kotlin, SQL migrations,
18	`application.yml`), KDoc and `// Why:` / `// Contract:` comments included. He is learning Kotlin
19	by writing it, so Claude does **not** write or edit files under `src/main/`, even when that would
20	be faster, and even inside `/feature`.
21	
22	Claude's job:
23	
24	- **Tests first.** Claude writes the tests under `src/test/` before Robert starts: one or more
25	  per acceptance criterion. They are the spec, and they fail until his code is right.

27	  in, and answer questions. When he's stuck, give hints in increasing order: the concept, then
28	  the API or annotation to look at, then the shape of the code in words. Show actual code only
29	  when he asks for it, and then as a snippet in chat for him to type, never as a file edit.
30	- **Review his code** when he asks: correctness against the contract and tests, idiomatic Kotlin,
31	  and the documentation standard. Explain each suggestion; he makes the change.
32	- **Everything around the code:** tests, study notes, README, TODO, build runs and tooling.
33	
34	Exception: Claude may edit `src/main/` only when Robert explicitly asks for that specific edit
35	in the current conversation. The `GET /inventory` code was written by Claude before this rule
36	existed (2026-09-24).
37	
38	## Source of truth
39	
40	- **API contract:** [src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml](src/main/resources/openapi/inventory.yaml). Paths, status codes,
41	  content types and schemas must match it exactly. Error responses (400/404) are
42	  `text/plain` strings, not JSON. `quantity` in requests has `minimum: 1`.
43	- If the contract is ambiguous (e.g. malformed JSON, missing body, SKU id format),
44	  stop and ask Robert rather than guessing; record the decision in the README.
45	
46	## Task list
47	
48	[.claude/TODO.md](.claude/TODO.md) is the working task list. Read it at the start of each session,
49	check items off as they are done, and add new items as they come up. Its **oversell protection
50	test plan** is a hard requirement: a purchase must never oversell, even under concurrent requests.
51	Every feature that touches stock must add or extend tests from that plan.
52	
53	## Stack
54	
55	- Kotlin on the JVM, Spring Boot (Spring MVC), Gradle with the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`).
56	  Chosen because it is what Nuuly runs in production.
57	- PostgreSQL (run with Docker Compose; Testcontainers in tests). Stock changes are single atomic
58	  SQL statements, backed by `CHECK (quantity >= 0)`. See the README decision record.
59	- Tests: JUnit Jupiter 6 (Spring Boot 4's version; same API as JUnit 5) with Spring's test support.
60	- Open decisions are tracked in the README under "Open decisions". Do not settle
61	  one silently; propose it, explain the trade-offs, and let Robert choose.
62	
63	## Documentation standard: clean code + study notes
64	
65	The code reads like good production code. The teaching lives in a **study-notes file per
66	source file** under [docs/learning/notes/](docs/learning/notes/README.md) (the README there
67	has the path mapping and format).
68	
69	**In the code:**
70	
71	1. **KDoc on every non-private declaration**: classes, interfaces, objects, and functions.
72	   Keep it short: what it does and where it sits in the request flow
73	   (controller → service → repository). Use `@param`, `@return`, and `@throws` only when
74	   they add information. Test classes get a KDoc saying what they cover.
75	   A PostToolUse hook ([scripts/check_kdoc.py](scripts/check_kdoc.py)) enforces this mechanically.
76	2. **Inline comments only for decisions and contract rules**, one or two lines each:
77	   - `// Why:` a design decision and the alternative that was rejected.
78	   - `// Contract:` the line exists to satisfy a specific part of inventory.yaml.
79	3. **First line links to the notes**: `// Study notes: docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`
80	   (`#` in YAML, `--` in SQL). `check_notes.py` verifies it.
81	4. **No teaching comments in code**: no `// Kotlin:` / `// Spring:` explanations, and no narration.
82	   Build files and `application.yml` may carry a one-line "what it's for" where it isn't obvious.
83	
84	**In the notes** (`docs/learning/notes/<mirrored path>.md`):
85	
86	1. Walk the file top to bottom in small chunks. **Quote each chunk** (don't reference line numbers)
87	   and explain it under `**Kotlin:**` (language features, with the Java equivalent when that
88	   helps), `**Spring:**` (framework behavior the code doesn't show), `**Why:**` and `**Contract:**`.
89	2. Explain a concept in full in the first notes file where it appears; elsewhere, link back to it.
90	   Index new concepts in [docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md](docs/learning/kotlin-concepts.md).
91	3. End with "Check your understanding" questions, without answers.
92	
93	**Keeping them in sync:** every code change updates its notes in the same piece of work. Run
94	`/sync-docs` to update them. A `Stop` hook ([scripts/check_notes.py](scripts/check_notes.py)) keeps
95	Claude working while any source file has changed more recently than its notes (or has none).

My role is tests first, then hints that escalate slowly (the concept, then the API to look up, then the shape of the code in words), with an actual snippet in chat only when you ask for one. After that I review your code, and I handle the docs.
- **[/feature](.claude/skills/feature/SKILL.md)** now runs: contract → plan → I write the failing tests → **you write the code while I coach** → review → notes. The notes describe your code after it passes. [/walkthrough](.claude/skills/walkthrough/SKILL.md) now has you explain your own code first, and I fill the gaps.
- **Enforcement: [scripts/code_guard.py](scripts/code_guard.py).** If I try to write anything under `src/main/`, Claude Code stops and asks you to approve it. That covers file edits and shell commands that write, move or delete files there. I tested 9 cases and all behaved correctly. Hook config is usually read at session start, so restart Claude Code once before relying on it.
- **Notes hook:** while `.claude/coding-in-progress` exists (gitignored), `check_notes` skips `src/main/`, so I won't try to document half-written code. `/sync-docs` removes the marker. I also fixed the hang I found earlier: hook mode is now an explicit `--hook` flag.
- **Memory:** a cross-session note records this rule and why.

**`GET /inventory` is back to square one for you:**
- I deleted my four Kotlin files, the migration, and their notes.
- My tests stay as your spec, and right now they won't compile. That's expected.
- The README shows the endpoint as "Tests written; Robert implementing". Your earlier decisions (sort by `sku_id`, include zero-stock SKUs, `TEXT`/`INTEGER` columns) still stand.
- The marker is set, so you're in coding mode.

**Your checklist**, in the order a request travels upward (all in package `com.robertwoolbright.inventory.inventory` unless noted):
1. `src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql`: the `inventory` table, with `sku_id` and `quantity` columns matching your decisions, and the rule that quantity can't go negative.
2. `InventoryItem`: holds a `skuId` (String) and a `quantity` (Int). The tests compare two of them with `==`, so think about which kind of class makes that work.
3. `InventoryRepository`: a Spring bean that gets a `JdbcClient` and has `findAll()`, returning every item sorted by SKU id.
4. `InventoryService`: `listInventory()`, which asks the repository.
5. `InventoryController`: handles `GET /inventory`.

Good first target: get `InventoryRepositoryTest` compiling and green (steps 1–3). Tell me when you want a build run, a hint, or a review.
